title: APIs for Agents: Rethinking API Programs in the MCP Era
gist: Morgan Stanley's API platform team (Jim Gough and Andreea Niculcea) describes a year-long shift from zero to over 110 production APIs deployed via 'Architecture as Code' (the FINOS open-source CALM framework), now extended to govern MCP servers and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocols with automated deployment gates, guardrails, and zero-downtime fleet-wide platform upgrades across 100+ API platforms and 400+ gateways, while arguing that stable, well-governed APIs remain the durable foundation beneath fast-churning AI protocol layers.

themes.theme: MCP fundamentals and why it differs from plain APIs

insights.claim: MCP is an open protocol for connecting LLM-based applications to tools and data, built around a cycle of discovering available capabilities, invoking them, and validating results; the protocol itself is architecturally simple client-server interaction with security and governance built in as near first-class concerns.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Establishes MCP as protocol-simple but ecosystem-complex, meaning investment should go into governance/orchestration layers around MCP rather than the protocol implementation itself.
insights.quote: It's an open protocol for connecting LLM-based applications to tools and data.
insights.locator: Introduction to MCP

insights.claim: MCP adds two elements beyond typical API/OpenAPI descriptions: prompts (reusable, parameterized instructions that guide behavior, important as multiple tools operate together) and resources (documents and data brought to agents for context) alongside tools (structured operations to perform a task).
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Clarifies the concrete technical differentiators of MCP versus OpenAPI (prompts + resources), which is the specific value-add enterprises are paying attention to versus a decade of existing API tooling.
insights.locator: What is it at the core? I mentioned tools

insights.claim: Gough observes that despite having had API specifications like OpenAPI for years, he has never seen anyone in the business get excited about an OpenAPI spec, while people are 'jumping up and down' about MCP specs and what they mean for the business.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A telling signal about enterprise adoption psychology: MCP's business-side excitement is driving budget and urgency in a way pure technical API improvements never did, explaining why MCP investment is accelerating despite technical overlap with existing API capabilities.
insights.quote: I've not seen anybody get really excited about an OpenAPI spec in the business. There are lots of people jumping up and down about MCP specs and what that means.
insights.locator: The key thing for me, as somebody who really believes in OpenAPI

insights.claim: The business demand signal behind MCP adoption is users wanting to 'talk to' technical products, trade information, and databases using natural language, including querying things they didn't even know existed within the technical estate.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Identifies natural-language discoverability of previously-siloed enterprise data as the core business driver of MCP demand, not just developer productivity — a useful lens for sizing enterprise MCP/agent tooling market demand.
insights.locator: The demand signal that we're seeing from the business

insights.claim: MCP timeline: announced November 2024; OpenAI started adopting MCP in 2025 (around the time of the prior year's QCon talk); GitHub then adopted it, driving broad developer day-to-day exposure; later, remote MCP servers became the dominant deployment model, which is the focus of Morgan Stanley's current work.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A concrete adoption timeline showing MCP went from announcement to OpenAI/GitHub adoption to enterprise production deployment (Morgan Stanley) in under two years, a rapid protocol-adoption curve worth benchmarking against other infra standards.
insights.locator: It's really new in terms of 2024, November, MCP was announced

insights.claim: MCP's real complexity is not the protocol itself but agent orchestration: as the number of exposed tools grows beyond roughly five, tool descriptions start overlapping, making disambiguation harder, which drives up cost because every extra tool read/response consumes tokens, creating a 'chatty' interaction pattern that has led to specialized gateways and control planes taking on more business-logic-aware responsibilities than traditional API gateways were meant to have.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Explains a concrete cost/scaling mechanism (tool-description overlap driving token cost) that any enterprise scaling MCP tool catalogs will hit, and predicts a new market segment for MCP-aware gateways/control planes distinct from classic API gateways.
insights.locator: Where's the complexity? I've said it's easy

insights.claim: CALM (Common Architecture Language Model) is an open-source FINOS (financial open source) project for 'Architecture as Code' that Morgan Stanley uses to power both its demos and its production architecture deployments; its core model is essentially a JSON schema for modeling boxes and arrows with typed information layered on top, plus CLI tooling, reusable 'patterns,' and CALM Hub (a central repository/discovery tool for architectures, patterns, and controls).
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Names a specific open-source governance framework (CALM/FINOS) enterprises can adopt rather than build in-house architecture-as-code tooling from scratch, relevant to any fintech or regulated-industry platform team evaluating AI-governance tooling.
insights.locator: It's an open-source project. It's from FINOS

insights.claim: CALM's 'patterns' encode reusable platform opinions as templates; Morgan Stanley has only three or four patterns in total but has used them for over 110 production deployments, giving developers guardrails and reuse while enforcing consistency.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A striking reuse ratio (roughly 30+ deployments per pattern) demonstrating that a small number of well-designed architecture templates can scale to serve a large, heterogeneous API portfolio — a concrete efficiency metric for platform engineering investment cases.
insights.locator: For us, we've got three or four patterns

insights.claim: CALM introduced 'decorators' to separate metadata and auxiliary information out of the core architecture definition, because architectures were becoming too heavy with people adding excessive metadata into one large JSON blob.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A practical schema-design lesson: as architecture-as-code schemas mature, teams need explicit mechanisms to decompose growing metadata rather than letting a single schema become unmanageable.
insights.locator: More recently, we've introduced something called decorators

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley built a model for non-functional requirements into CALM covering areas like MCP, observability, and performance, deliberately left open as a community-contributed model rather than a small closed team like Gough's defining every standard; on top of this, 'control requirements' and 'configurations' let teams specify and enforce architecture-level guardrails (e.g., denying certain symbols from being queried via MCP, or requiring network segmentation).
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A governance pattern (requirement + configuration pairs, enforced automatically at the architecture layer) directly transferable to any enterprise building MCP governance — avoids bespoke, ad hoc compliance checks per deployment.
insights.locator: We ended up building in something which is a model for non-functional requirements

insights.claim: In a live demo, Morgan Stanley added a denied-symbols guardrail directly on an MCP server (not the underlying REST API); when queried again, the MCP tool call returned an explicit 'symbol is restricted and cannot be queried' error advising the user to contact compliance — the guardrail was deliberately deployed at the MCP layer, generated automatically from CALM architecture/control definitions into a Kubernetes ConfigMap consumed at runtime by the MCP server's Java code.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A concrete, reproducible pattern for compliance-driven access control at the AI-agent tool layer (not just the underlying API) — a template for regulated industries needing auditable AI guardrails.
insights.quote: your symbol is restricted and cannot be queried. You'll want to contact your compliance team to find out why this has happened.
insights.locator: Interesting, our Trades Connector is now returning an error

insights.claim: Gough later reveals the Vodafone-symbol guardrail was deliberately placed in the MCP server rather than the underlying API specifically to illustrate a design question — where controls should live — and states the correct answer is the API layer, because placing a control in the API means it doesn't need to be re-implemented if new consumer protocols (like A2A) are added later.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A specific, non-obvious architectural best practice: security/business controls should be enforced in the stable API layer, not in fast-churning protocol adapters like MCP or A2A, to avoid duplicating controls across every new interaction protocol.
insights.quote: You want to keep your controls where they belong, APIs or API gateways.
insights.locator: Interestingly, you will notice that we put the guardrail

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley's platform enforces multi-stage deployment gates: pattern-conformance checks (rejecting architectures that don't reference an approved pattern), CALM CLI-based architecture validation (JSON schema validation plus spectral-based checks catching missing placeholders like image versions or missing relationship controls), followed later by smoke tests, API standards checks, entitlement checks, security reviews with drift detection, and synthetic-monitoring traffic health checks before and after production push.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A detailed, reusable staged-gate pipeline (pattern check -> schema/spectral validation -> smoke/API standards/entitlements -> security review/drift detection -> synthetic monitoring) that other platform teams can use as a governance blueprint for agentic/API deployments.
insights.locator: The first thing we want to do is generate our deployer

insights.claim: Gough argues platform value comes from removing decisions developers would otherwise have to repeatedly and independently make (API standards, security controls, observability implementation, audit requirements); leaving these to individual teams increases developer cognitive load and causes architectural consistency across the organization to degrade over time, whereas self-service with guardrails provides a 'paved road' encoding institutional knowledge for teams to rediscover, not redesign, each time.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A clear articulation of the platform-engineering value thesis with a causal mechanism (decision fatigue -> architectural drift) that justifies continued investment in centralized, encoded platform guardrails over team autonomy.
insights.quote: The real value of a platform comes when it can remove decisions that our developers have to make repeatedly and independently.
insights.locator: This is where deployment gates come in

insights.claim: Agent-driven traffic breaks the traditional transactional capacity-planning model (client request -> service processes -> response, sized by requests-per-second and average latency); a single natural-language question can expand into dozens of chained tool calls across multiple MCP servers (e.g., trades, portfolio exposure, trading analysis, risk policy, compliance checks), with retries, reordering, and partial failures, meaning MCP tool calls require substantially more platform responsibility than a REST request, including JSON schema validation, pagination, output shaping, and workflow management.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A concrete operational thesis that traditional RPS/latency-based capacity planning is insufficient for agentic workloads; infra teams need new SLA and cost models accounting for chained, retrying, variable-fan-out tool call patterns — directly relevant to how cloud/API platform vendors should redesign pricing and monitoring for agent traffic.
insights.locator: Agents don't behave like that

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley's 'operational rollout' mechanism lets the platform team push new platform opinions (e.g., reacting to a Log4Shell-style event or patching all Envoy proxies) as an updated CALM template, then redeploy all existing architectures through it, rather than relying on 100+ individual teams to self-initiate hygiene-program updates; because CALM Hub maintains the golden source of what's deployed and where, the team can now patch across the entire estate — cited as over 400 gateways — within an hour without downtime for consumers.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A striking, concrete operational capability (patch 400+ gateways within an hour, zero downtime) that quantifies the operational leverage gained from architecture-as-code — a strong ROI data point for security/incident-response speed in regulated finance environments.
insights.quote: We've done things now where we can roll across the entire estate and patch something within an hour across 400-plus gateways without having to have any downtime for our consumers.
insights.locator: Security and policy and governance must be built into a platform

insights.claim: Since the start of the year, Morgan Stanley has performed zero-downtime infrastructure upgrades across its 100+ API platforms in production by issuing a new platform opinion (e.g., removing a cluster from routine configuration) as a CALM template, redeploying all architectures through the same controls a user-initiated deployment would go through, isolating one cluster (e.g., leaving 3 of 4 clusters serving traffic) to perform the upgrade, then repeating the process to bring it back into rotation.
insights.speaker: Andreea Niculcea
insights.so_what: A concrete production pattern for zero-downtime fleet-wide infra upgrades using rolling cluster isolation driven entirely by declarative platform-opinion changes — a reusable operational playbook for large multi-cluster platform teams.
insights.locator: Only since the beginning of this year, I think

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley's platform team demonstrated live evolution of platform opinion by pushing a new CALM 'bundle' (v2) that adds pod resource limits to the MCP server deployment; re-running CALM template against the existing conforming architecture applied the new opinion without requiring the application team to change anything themselves.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the mechanism (bundle diff -> re-template -> redeploy) by which platform-wide policy changes (like adding missing pod resource limits, a common production hygiene gap) propagate without per-team action — reduces a common source of production incidents (unbounded resource pods).
insights.locator: We can check the diff in here

themes.theme: Adoption speed, ROI, and strategic positioning

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley's first API took about two years to get to a 'hello world' due to the various architecture hoops required; this was reduced to six months per new API, and with recent CALM-driven automatic security approvals, has come down further to roughly one to two weeks per new API.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A dramatic, quantified time-to-market improvement (2 years -> 6 months -> 1-2 weeks) directly attributable to automated architecture-as-code governance, a compelling ROI case study for CALM/Architecture-as-Code investment in large regulated enterprises.
insights.locator: We eventually got that down to it being six months

insights.claim: Gough frames current AI-driven change as forcing enterprises out of the traditional Thoughtworks Radar 'adopt' phase (mature, vendor-supported, well-understood technology) into 'assess' or 'trial and assess' as the new normal standard for adopting new capabilities, which he characterizes as inherently risky since some bets will work and some will become outdated quickly, including uncertainty about whether MCP itself will remain the dominant protocol by year end.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A senior enterprise architect explicitly flags protocol risk — MCP's own dominance is not assumed to be permanent — implying enterprises should architect for protocol substitutability rather than betting infrastructure on MCP specifically persisting.
insights.quote: Who knows if MCP will be around at the end of this year?
insights.locator: In terms of artificial intelligence, it's really driving bleeding-edge adoption

insights.claim: Gough's central strategic thesis is that APIs remain the stable contract layer beneath fast-moving AI tooling (new models, prompts, tool-use patterns, skills); if experimentation and rapid protocol adoption (MCP today, A2A tomorrow) is anchored behind well-built, best-practice APIs, an organization has a robust foundation to adapt to whatever comes next, whereas building new protocol adapters without those foundations risks ending up in 'a potentially sticky situation down the road.'
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Core investable thesis: the durable long-term value in the AI agent infrastructure stack accrues to stable, well-governed API layers, not to whichever protocol (MCP, A2A, or a future successor) is fashionable at a given time — informs how to evaluate 'AI infrastructure' vendors by whether they reinforce or bypass API governance.
insights.quote: APIs remaining as the key building blocks is a safe bet to have.
insights.locator: This is a bit of my plug for APIs

insights.claim: Network segmentation and pod-level isolation are framed as critical risk mitigation for rapid AI-driven adoption because if a component (including third-party open-source dependencies in the supply chain) is compromised, isolation contains the blast radius, allowing Morgan Stanley to safely adopt fast-moving, less-proven technologies without full traditional governance review cycles upfront.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Network micro-segmentation is positioned as the enabling control that lets a regulated enterprise take on higher technology risk (adopting unproven AI protocols/tools) safely — a key architectural prerequisite other regulated firms should replicate before fast-tracking AI adoption.
insights.locator: When it comes to things like network segmentation

insights.claim: Gough distinguishes MCP and A2A architecturally: MCP centers on tool calls and a standard invocation interaction, whereas A2A removes the concept of calling a tool in favor of independent systems discovering each other and coordinating via message exchanges built on tasks — Gough compares the A2A discovery/coordination model to Akka with additional features layered on top.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A clear technical distinction (tool-invocation vs. agent-discovery-and-coordination) useful for architects deciding when to expose capabilities via MCP tools versus A2A agent cards, and a notable comparison point to existing actor-model systems like Akka.
insights.locator: MCPs are much more around making tool calls

insights.claim: In a live A2A demo, a Python rebalancer script observed a portfolio via a Trades A2A agent, detected a change (5.2% NVDA position appearing after new trade bookings) using a simple decision tree, and automatically booked new trades to rebalance — Gough notes that a more genuinely agentic design would instead let the agent itself decide whether rebalancing is needed, rather than hard-coding the decision logic in the script, and admits he would architect the MCP/A2A combination differently if building it again.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: An honest admission that even a leading enterprise implementation currently uses scripted decision logic rather than true agentic decision-making for A2A, and that the team's own architecture would change on a second iteration — signals the space is still architecturally immature even among sophisticated early adopters.
insights.locator: Architecturally, what's interesting with agent-to-agent

insights.claim: Adding an A2A adapter onto the existing trades/MCP demo required minimal additional work because the underlying API and Kubernetes cluster (already micro-segmented and secured with MCP and API servers) simply had an A2A server added in front, illustrating that new protocol adapters can be layered onto an existing well-governed API foundation with relatively low incremental effort.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Empirical validation of the 'APIs as stable foundation' thesis: a new protocol (A2A) was added to production infrastructure quickly because governance and security were already encoded at the API/platform layer rather than needing to be rebuilt per-protocol.
insights.locator: Again, this is all added into, if you were to look at the Kubernetes cluster now

insights.claim: Gough notes AI introduces many new categories of API consumers beyond system-to-system calls — developers directly tinkering, apps, and agents — and that developer experimentation in particular causes traffic volumes and spikes to increase rapidly (sometimes before a business question is even fully answered), changing traffic patterns, retry behavior, and API usage patterns the platform must accommodate.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: Highlights an underappreciated capacity-planning risk: internal developer experimentation with AI tools/agents can itself become a major, unpredictable source of traffic load distinct from customer-facing demand.
insights.locator: AI changes things, though. It introduces a lot of new consumers

insights.claim: In audience Q&A, Gough describes two adoption modes for CALM within Morgan Stanley: centrally-managed platform components (Kubernetes clusters, service mesh, API managers) that developers configure via CALM-defined opinions, versus using CALM templates and tooling to bootstrap new projects from scratch (e.g., invoking Spring Initializer or Quarkus Start with baseline configuration) so a team can go straight to a working production baseline and then iterate — he notes this involves losing some flexibility in exchange for significant productivity gains, and that developers tend to prefer tweaking something already working in production over building from zero.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A candid trade-off framework (centralized configuration vs. project-bootstrapping) for how large organizations can introduce architecture-as-code governance without provoking developer resistance — useful playbook for change management in platform-engineering rollouts.
insights.locator: I think there are two different ways you can do this

insights.claim: Gough describes CALM as originally a risky bet — his boss asked whether he was sure about putting an open-source project at the center of everything Morgan Stanley was doing, roughly a year before this talk — and Gough says he is glad they did it, given being lead maintainers let them 'fix it in the open source and make it work,' turning what was a part-time project into what is now effectively a full-time commitment.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A candid institutional risk-taking narrative: a major regulated bank chose to become lead maintainer of a young open-source project central to its core infrastructure rather than build/buy proprietary tooling, a strategic bet that appears to have paid off given the subsequent scale (110+ deployments, 400+ gateways).
insights.locator: We're the lead maintainers on there

insights.claim: Gough cites industry reports that platform teams often spend roughly 70% of their time on undifferentiated heavy lifting (e.g., Terraform and infrastructure work) and only about 30% on business logic, framing well-designed platform guardrails as the fix that shifts this balance back toward differentiated work.
insights.speaker: Jim Gough
insights.so_what: A cited industry pain-point statistic (70/30 split toward undifferentiated infra work) that quantifies the opportunity cost platform engineering investment is meant to recover — useful benchmark for evaluating platform-engineering ROI claims broadly.
insights.locator: There's lots of documentation about folks who are spending way too much time
